bib.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 33rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), New York, NY, USA, 2016

read.skipped: The full theoretical appendix (derivations, sections 2-4, D.1, E.1, E.2) is not in this PDF; it is hosted at arXiv 1506.02157 (the PDF only has Table 2 as appendix). Setup details in E.1/E.2 are therefore unrecorded.

question: Can dropout training in neural networks be interpreted as approximate Bayesian inference in a deep Gaussian process, so that existing dropout networks yield model uncertainty at test time?
hypothesis: Keeping dropout active at test time and averaging T stochastic forward passes (MC dropout) gives useful predictive mean and uncertainty without changing the model or its optimisation.
contributions: Theory: a NN of arbitrary depth with dropout before every weight layer is equivalent to an approximation to a deep GP; the dropout objective minimises KL to the GP posterior
MC dropout: predictive mean, variance and log-likelihood estimators from T stochastic forward passes
Empirical study of uncertainty across architectures and non-linearities (ReLU vs TanH), MNIST classification, UCI regression benchmarks, and a reinforcement learning use

method.summary: Theory casts dropout training as variational inference with a Bernoulli q(w); at test time T stochastic forward passes give mean and variance, with model precision tau tied to weight decay by tau = p l^2 / (2 N lambda). Evaluated on CO2 extrapolation, rotated MNIST digit with LeNet, 10 UCI regression sets vs VI and PBP, and Thompson sampling in a 2D RL task.

training.objective: L2-regularised loss (eq. 1), equal to the GP KL objective for suitable tau and l; softmax loss for classification, square loss for regression
training.optimizer: Adam (UCI); Caffe reference solver for MNIST
training.lr_schedule: MNIST: same policy as 'before' with gamma=0.0001, p=0.75 (earlier definition not in this PDF)
training.steps: MNIST: 10^6 iterations; UCI: Bayesian optimisation 40 iterations, then 10x more epochs for the final model
training.epochs: UCI: 10x the 40 epochs of PBP (Table 1); 100x in the Table 2 '10x Epochs' variant
training.weight_decay: lambda = p l^2 / (2 N tau); UCI prior length-scale l = 10^-2 for most datasets, tau found by Bayesian optimisation on validation log-likelihood
training.compute: Naval Propulsion: 276 s per split including BO, 95 s without; PBP 220 s. Kin8nm: 188 s with BO, 65 s without; PBP 156 s

other.software: Keras on Theano (UCI); Caffe (MNIST); convnetjs code (RL)

inference.decoding: MC dropout: T stochastic forward passes, average for mean (eq. 6), sample variance plus tau^-1 for variance
inference.samples: T=1000 for CO2 figures (T=10 in Fig 3); 100 stochastic forward passes scattered for MNIST; RL uses a single forward pass per action (Thompson sampling); T for UCI not stated

parameters.predictive_log_likelihood: logsumexp(-0.5 tau ||y - yhat_t||^2) - log T - 0.5 log 2pi + 0.5 log tau

limits: Full derivations and setup details (E.1, E.2, D.1) live in an external appendix, arXiv 1506.02157, and are not in this PDF.
Predictive distribution is highly multi-modal; the moment-matching estimates are only a glimpse of it.
Uncertainty quality depends on the nonlinearity and weight-regularisation choice, which fix the GP covariance; study left to future work.
UCI dropout probabilities (0.05, 0.005) and tau were tuned by Bayesian optimisation; networks were small; RMSE better on only 9 of 10 sets (Yacht exception).
In RL, the dropout agent stops improving after about 1K batches because it still samples random moves.
Standard errors in the earlier arXiv version were scaled up by 4.5 (corrected Oct 2016); results rest on one RL run.
Later work disputes whether the Bayesian interpretation yields calibrated posteriors; the paper itself does not test calibration directly beyond LL.
